summary: The article provides a largely accurate overview of IPO taxation in India, including STCG and LTCG, ITR filing, and advance tax, incorporating recent changes from the Union Budget 2024-25. However, there are a few inaccuracies regarding the STCG tax rate and the basic exemption limit for STCG.

claims.claim: STCG on listed equity is currently taxed at 20% under Section 111A, provided Securities Transaction Tax (STT) is paid.
claims.note: Multiple sources confirm that STCG on listed equity is taxed at 20% under Section 111A, effective from July 23, 2024, provided STT is paid.

claims.claim: LTCG on listed equity is taxed at 12.5% on gains exceeding ₹1.25 lakh under Section 112A, with STT paid.
claims.note: Sources confirm that LTCG on listed equity is taxed at 12.5% on gains exceeding ₹1.25 lakh under Section 112A, effective from July 23, 2024, with STT paid.

claims.claim: Effective from July 23, 2024, the tax rate for such gains has been increased to 20%, provided Securities Transaction Tax (STT) has been paid on both the acquisition and sale of these shares.
claims.note: The Union Budget 2024-25, presented on July 23, 2024, increased the STCG tax rate on listed equity shares to 20% under Section 111A, contingent on STT being paid.

claims.claim: it is important to note that unlike some other income types, there is no basic exemption limit for STCG on listed equity shares; every rupee of such gain is taxable at the specified rate. This means that even if your total taxable income is below the basic exemption limit, STCG will still be taxed at 20%.
claims.note: While STCG under Section 111A is taxed at a special rate, a resident individual can adjust the gain against any unused basic exemption limit. Only the remaining STCG, after this adjustment, is taxed at the applicable rate. However, non-residents are not allowed to claim the basic exemption limit for STCG under Section 111A.

claims.claim: Under Section 112A of the Income Tax Act, LTCG on listed equity shares (including IPO shares) is taxed at a concessional rate. As per the Union Budget 2024-25, effective from July 23, 2024, the tax rate for LTCG exceeding an exemption threshold has been revised to 12.5%, provided STT has been paid on the transaction. A significant benefit here is the exemption limit: the first ₹1.25 lakh of LTCG on listed equity shares in a financial year is entirely exempt from tax. Only the gains exceeding this ₹1.25 lakh threshold are taxed at 12.5%.
claims.note: The Union Budget 2024-25, effective July 23, 2024, increased the LTCG tax rate to 12.5% and the exemption limit to ₹1.25 lakh under Section 112A for listed equity shares, provided STT is paid.

claims.claim: For shares acquired before January 31, 2018, a 'grandfathering clause' is applicable, which protects gains accrued until that date from taxation. The cost of acquisition for such shares is considered as the higher of the actual purchase price or the Fair Market Value (FMV) as of January 31, 2018 (subject to the sale price not exceeding the FMV).
claims.note: The grandfathering clause for shares acquired before January 31, 2018, is correctly described, allowing the cost of acquisition to be the higher of the actual purchase price or the FMV as of January 31, 2018 (subject to sale price not exceeding FMV).

claims.claim: If your capital gains from IPOs or other sources are substantial, you might also have an advance tax liability. Advance tax is payable in instalments if your estimated tax liability for the year exceeds ₹10,000. Failure to pay advance tax or paying less than the required amount can lead to interest under Sections 234B and 234C of the Income Tax Act.
claims.note: Advance tax is indeed payable if the estimated tax liability exceeds ₹10,000, and interest under Sections 234B and 234C can be levied for non-compliance.

claims.claim: Short-term capital losses (STCL) can be set off against both STCG and LTCG. Long-term capital losses (LTCL) can only be set off against LTCG. Unadjusted losses can be carried forward for up to eight assessment years.
claims.note: The rules for setting off and carrying forward capital losses are accurately stated.
